title: Choking, seizures and physical first aid
blurb: Act fast and in the right order for choking, seizures, chest pain, low glucose, bleeding, burns and opioid overdose.
question: Mr Okafor, 67, is eating lunch in the ward day room when he suddenly clutches his throat. He cannot speak or cough but is still conscious. Help has been called. What should the nurse do next?

teach.h: First aid: the first link in the chain
teach.body: First aid is any helping behaviour, by anyone, for any emergency: recognise the problem, prioritise, act within your competence and get help early. Resuscitation Council UK (RCUK) 2025 sets three principles: check the scene is safe, call for help (999 in the community, 2222 in most hospitals) and use only equipment and medicines you are trained to use. In plain English: keep yourself safe, shout early, then fix the most dangerous problem first using ABCDE.

steps.label:
Ask "Are you
choking?"
steps.sub: Sudden inability to speak or cough, often while eating

steps.label: Effective cough?
steps.sub: Yes: encourage coughing and watch closely

steps.label:
Up to 5
abdominal thrusts
steps.sub: If back blows fail; then alternate 5 and 5

steps.label: Unresponsive?
steps.sub: Start CPR and make sure help is coming

teach.caption: No blind finger sweeps. Anyone given abdominal thrusts should be checked by a clinician afterwards.

teach.body: A person who can cough forcefully, speak or breathe has a mild obstruction: their own cough is the best tool, so encourage it and stay with them. A person who cannot cough, speak or breathe has a severe obstruction and needs back blows straight away. If the person becomes unresponsive, the airway problem has become a cardiac arrest risk: start CPR, because chest compressions also raise pressure in the airway.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Okafor in the day room
teach.body: Mr Okafor cannot speak or cough, so his obstruction is severe. The nurse stands to his side and slightly behind, supports his chest, leans him forward and gives up to five sharp back blows between the shoulder blades, checking after each one. If the food does not clear, she gives up to five abdominal thrusts, then alternates. Once it clears she records what happened and asks the doctor to examine him, because thrusts can cause internal injury.

head: Emergency
Key first action

15–20 g glucose tablets if awake and can swallow
Repeat oral glucose; snack once recovered
Nothing by mouth; call 999; recovery position
Call for help; CPR if not breathing normally; naloxone if trained
teach.caption: RCUK 2025 First aid guidelines.

teach.h: A convulsive seizure: what to do

root.label: Tonic-clonic seizure
root.sub: Protect, time it, do not restrain

children.label: Cushion head, clear area
children.sub: Nothing in the mouth; note start time

children.label: Recovery position
children.sub: Stay and talk calmly until recovered

children.label: Emergency
children.sub: Follow their plan; call for help or 999

teach.caption: NICE NG217: convulsive status epilepticus means seizures lasting 5 minutes or more. Give emergency medicine as in the person's individual plan; without a plan, buccal midazolam or rectal diazepam in the community, or IV lorazepam where IV access and resuscitation facilities are available (recs 7.1.2 to 7.1.3).

items.label: back blows, then abdominal thrusts, for severe choking
aspirin, chewed, for cardiac-sounding chest pain
cool running water on a burn or scald
above a limb wound for a tourniquet, not over a joint

teach.caption: Sources: RCUK 2025 First aid guidelines; NHS burns and scalds advice (reviewed 2026).

items: Life-threatening bleeding: firm direct pressure, ideally over a haemostatic dressing, then a pressure dressing once controlled.
Limb bleeding not controlled by pressure: tourniquet 5–7 cm above the wound, tightened until bleeding stops; write down the time and do not release it.
Burns and scalds: cool running water for 20 minutes; remove nearby clothing or jewellery unless stuck to the skin.
Then lay cling film over the burn (do not wrap it round); no creams, butter or sticky dressings.
Large, deep, facial, genital, chemical or electrical burns need emergency care.

teach.text: Two classic errors: putting something in the mouth of a person having a seizure (never: it causes injury and does not stop tongue biting), and giving sugar by mouth to someone who is drowsy and cannot swallow safely (aspiration risk). Also, the recovery position is for reduced responsiveness with normal breathing, not for agonal gasping (that is cardiac arrest) or suspected trauma.

items: Scene safety, call for help early, act within your training (RCUK 2025).
Choking: effective cough = encourage; ineffective = 5 back blows then 5 abdominal thrusts; unresponsive = CPR.
Chest pain: 300 mg aspirin chewed unless allergic. Hypo below 4.0 mmol/L: 15–20 g glucose, repeat after 15 minutes.
Seizure: protect, time, nothing in the mouth, recovery position after; 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus (NG217).
Bleeding: direct pressure, then tourniquet 5–7 cm above. Burns: 20 minutes cool running water, then cling film.

summary: You can now work through the adult choking algorithm in order, manage a seizure safely and recognise status epilepticus at 5 minutes. You can also give the correct first aid for chest pain, hypoglycaemia, opioid overdose, severe bleeding and burns.

A.q: Mrs Patel, 72, is eating in a hospital café when she starts choking. She is coughing hard, is red in the face and can say a few words. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give up to five back blows between her shoulder blades
Give up to five abdominal thrusts below her ribcage
Encourage her to keep coughing and stay with her
Look in her mouth and sweep out any visible food
A.why: A forceful cough with the ability to speak means a mild obstruction. RCUK 2025 advises encouraging the cough and watching for deterioration to an ineffective cough.

whyNot.0: Back blows are for an ineffective cough; they could interrupt an effective one.
whyNot.1: Abdominal thrusts come after back blows have failed in a severe obstruction.
whyNot.3: RCUK 2025 advises against blind finger sweeps, which can push the object further in.

A.q: Mr Hughes, 58, a visitor on a cardiology ward, develops central crushing chest pain. He is alert, has no allergies and help is on the way. Which action is most appropriate while waiting?
options: Help him chew 300 mg aspirin and stay with him
Give him 75 mg aspirin to swallow with water
Walk him to the emergency department straight away
Give him a sugary drink in case it is hypoglycaemia
A.why: RCUK 2025 first aid: for cardiac-sounding chest pain, help the person self-administer 300 mg aspirin, ideally chewed, unless allergic, and stay with them.

whyNot.1: 75 mg is a maintenance dose; the first aid dose is 300 mg, chewed for faster absorption.
whyNot.2: Walking increases cardiac workload; he should rest in a comfortable position while help comes to him.
whyNot.3: Nothing suggests hypoglycaemia; delaying aspirin for a sugary drink misses the priority.

A.q: Lucy, 26, has a tonic-clonic seizure in an outpatient waiting area. She is on the floor next to a metal chair. What should the nurse do first?
options: Hold her arms and legs still to stop her injuring herself
Move the chair away, cushion her head and note the time
Place a padded airway between her teeth to protect her tongue
Roll her into the recovery position while she is convulsing
A.why: NHS seizure first aid: move away dangerous objects, cushion the head, loosen tight clothing and time the seizure; turn the person on their side once convulsions stop.

whyNot.0: Restraining a person during a seizure can cause injury and does not shorten it.
whyNot.2: Nothing should be put in the mouth during a seizure, including fingers or airways.
whyNot.3: The recovery position is used after the convulsions have stopped, not during them.

B.q: Mr Davies, 70, has type 2 diabetes and is shaky and sweaty. He is alert and can swallow. His capillary glucose is 3.1 mmol/L. Which action is most appropriate first?
options: Give 15–20 g of glucose tablets and recheck afterwards
Give his next meal now and recheck in one hour
Ask him to rest and repeat the glucose in 30 minutes
Give a glucose gel and lie him in the recovery position
B.why: RCUK 2025: a conscious person who can swallow with glucose below 4.0 mmol/L should have 15–20 g glucose tablets, with a repeat measurement after treatment.

whyNot.1: A meal is too slow to correct hypoglycaemia; a snack comes after recovery.
whyNot.2: Waiting without treatment risks further fall in glucose and loss of consciousness.
whyNot.3: He is alert and can swallow, so tablets are first choice; the recovery position is for reduced responsiveness.

B.q: Ben, 31, has a deep thigh wound after a fall through a glass door at a clinic. Bright red blood keeps soaking through despite firm direct pressure. A tourniquet is available and the nurse is trained. Where should it be placed?
options: Directly over the wound to compress the bleeding vessel
Over the knee joint just below the wound for a firm grip
5–7 cm above the wound, avoiding any joint
At the top of the thigh close to the groin crease
B.why: RCUK 2025: for life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by direct pressure, place a tourniquet 5–7 cm above the injury, not over a joint, tighten until bleeding stops and record the time.

whyNot.0: A tourniquet works by compressing the limb above the wound, not on top of it.
whyNot.1: A tourniquet should not go over a joint, and below the wound will not stop arterial flow into it.
whyNot.3: RCUK 2025 specifies 5–7 cm above the injury rather than as high as possible.

B.q: Amira, 40, spilt boiling water over her forearm in a staff kitchen 5 minutes ago. The skin is red and blistering. Which first aid is most appropriate?
options: Apply an ice pack wrapped in a cloth for 10 minutes
Cool it under cool running water for 20 minutes
Apply a moisturising cream and a sticky dressing
Cover it with a dry dressing and leave it to cool
B.why: NHS advice: hold a burn or scald under cool running water for 20 minutes as soon as possible, then lay cling film over it.

whyNot.0: Cool running water, not ice, is recommended; ice can further damage injured skin.
whyNot.2: Creams and sticky dressings should not be put on burns.
whyNot.3: Covering without cooling misses the 20 minutes of cool running water that limits damage.

C.q: Joel, 24, is found on a ward toilet floor. He is very drowsy, breathing 6 times a minute with pinpoint pupils, and a used syringe lies nearby. Help has been called. The nurse is trained to give naloxone. Which sequence is most appropriate?
options: Recovery position, then wait for the medical team to prescribe
Check his capillary glucose before deciding on any treatment
Give rescue breaths and leave naloxone to the doctor
Open the airway, support breathing and give naloxone
C.why: Slow breathing, extreme drowsiness and pinpoint pupils suggest opioid overdose. RCUK 2025: call for help, start CPR if not breathing normally, give naloxone if trained and reassess with ABCDE.

whyNot.0: With a respiratory rate of 6 he needs his breathing supported and naloxone now, not a wait.
whyNot.1: Glucose is worth checking later in D of ABCDE, but it should not delay airway and breathing support.
whyNot.2: Breaths help, but RCUK 2025 advises a trained rescuer to give naloxone for suspected opioid overdose rather than wait.

C.q: Grace, 45, has known epilepsy and an individual emergency plan with buccal midazolam. She has a tonic-clonic seizure at a day centre. After 5 minutes she is still convulsing. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Wait until 10 minutes before giving any medicine
Give her buccal midazolam as set out in her plan
Place her in the recovery position and keep timing
Give her oral diazepam once the jerking slows down
C.why: NICE NG217 defines convulsive status epilepticus as seizures lasting 5 minutes or more and says to give medication as detailed in the person's individual emergency management plan.

whyNot.0: NG217 uses 5 minutes, not 10, as the point for emergency treatment.
whyNot.2: She is still convulsing at 5 minutes, so emergency medicine is due now, not more observation.
whyNot.3: Nothing should be given by mouth during a seizure; her plan uses the buccal route.

C.q: Peter, 63, is choking on a piece of meat in a care home. Five back blows and five abdominal thrusts have not cleared it. He is still conscious. A colleague has gone for help but 999 has not been called. What should happen now?
options: Call 999 and keep alternating back blows and thrusts
Lie him on the floor and begin chest compressions now
Give him water to sip to wash the obstruction down
Try blind finger sweeps between rounds of thrusts
C.why: RCUK 2025: if choking is not relieved after five abdominal thrusts, call 999 and continue alternating five back blows with five abdominal thrusts until relieved or the person becomes unresponsive.

whyNot.1: Compressions start if he becomes unresponsive; while conscious he still needs back blows and thrusts.
whyNot.2: Drinking with a severe obstruction risks aspiration and will not clear the airway.
whyNot.3: RCUK 2025 specifically advises against blind finger sweeps.

reteach.title: Escalate one step at a time
reteach.question: Most first aid algorithms are ladders: you start with the least invasive step and climb only if it fails. How does that work for choking, bleeding and hypoglycaemia?

blocks.body: RCUK 2025 describes choking and bleeding care as an escalating approach. For choking: cough, then back blows, then abdominal thrusts, then CPR. For bleeding: direct pressure, then a haemostatic dressing, then a tourniquet. For low glucose: oral glucose, repeat after 15 minutes, then emergency help if no better or if the person becomes unresponsive. You move up a rung only when the one below is not working.

blocks.text: Skipping a rung is as risky as stopping too early: abdominal thrusts before back blows, or a tourniquet before trying firm pressure, add harm without adding benefit.

explain.body: Ask "Are you choking?" Effective cough: encourage it. Ineffective cough and conscious: up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, alternating; call 999 if not relieved. Unresponsive: start CPR. No blind finger sweeps.

test.q: Kwame, 50, cannot cough or speak after inhaling a sweet but is conscious. What should the nurse give first?
options: Up to 5 back blows
Up to 5 abdominal thrusts
Up to 5 chest thrusts
Two rescue breaths
test.why: For a conscious adult with an ineffective cough, RCUK 2025 starts with up to five back blows.

whyNot.1: Abdominal thrusts follow if back blows fail.
whyNot.2: Chest thrusts are not the first step in the adult algorithm.
whyNot.3: Rescue breaths are part of CPR once a person is unresponsive.

explain.body: Protect from injury, cushion the head, loosen tight clothing, time it and put nothing in the mouth. Recovery position once convulsions stop. Call for help if it is a first seizure, lasts longer than usual or 5 minutes if unknown, or repeats without recovery.

test.q: Under NICE NG217, convulsive status epilepticus is a seizure lasting at least how long?
options: 2 minutes
10 minutes
5 minutes
30 minutes
test.why: NG217 rec 7.1.1 defines convulsive status epilepticus as seizures lasting 5 minutes or more.

whyNot.0: 2 minutes longer than usual defines a prolonged seizure, not status epilepticus.
whyNot.1: 10 minutes is too long: NG217 starts emergency treatment for status epilepticus at 5 minutes.
whyNot.3: 30 minutes was the old definition, replaced by 5 minutes.

explain.body: Cardiac-sounding chest pain: rest, call for help, 300 mg aspirin chewed unless allergic. Glucose below 4.0 mmol/L and able to swallow: 15–20 g glucose, repeat after 15 minutes. Opioid overdose: slow breathing, pinpoint pupils; support breathing and give naloxone if trained.

test.q: Rosa, 77, is hypoglycaemic and responds only to pain. Which action is correct?
options: Give glucose gel inside her cheek pouch
Give 150 mL of fruit juice
Give two glucose tablets
Give nothing by mouth and get help
test.why: RCUK 2025: in an unresponsive person, give no oral sugar in any form because of aspiration risk; call for help and consider the recovery position.

whyNot.0: Gel is for a person who is awake; with reduced responsiveness it can be aspirated.
whyNot.1: She cannot swallow safely, so juice risks aspiration.
whyNot.2: Tablets need a person who is awake and able to swallow.

explain.body: Bleeding: direct pressure, haemostatic dressing, then a tourniquet 5–7 cm above a limb wound, time noted, not released by first aiders. Burns: 20 minutes cool running water, remove unstuck jewellery and clothing, lay cling film over, no creams.

test.q: After cooling a scald on Jonah's hand for 20 minutes, how should it be covered?
options: A layer of cling film laid over it
A cream and a sticky plaster
Cling film wrapped firmly around the hand
A dry gauze pad and tape
test.why: NHS advice: once cooled, lay cling film over the burn; do not wrap it round, and do not use creams or sticky dressings.

whyNot.1: Creams and sticky dressings should not be used on burns.
whyNot.2: Wrapping can constrict as the hand swells; it should be laid over.
whyNot.3: Gauze can stick to a burn; cling film is advised.
